answer.label: Not William Butler Yeats — an anonymous mid-century saying
answer.authorDates: 1881–1959 · British-born American newspaper poet, “the People’s Poet”
answer.sourceLine: No verified Yeats poem, play, letter, or prose work contains this line. Quote Investigator ↗ traces the sentiment to Edgar Guest’s 1915 poem “Faith” and 1919 poem “The Unknown Friends,” while close anonymous variants (“strangers are just friends you haven’t met up with yet”) ran as U.S. newspaper filler by 1941 and the “no strangers, only friends” construction is documented from 1951; the saying was first pinned on Yeats in an uncited 1997 Usenet post.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: No identified single author; evolved anonymously

source.excerpt: There are no strangers here; only friends you haven't yet met.
trail: In 1915 Edgar Guest published the poem “Faith,” which included the line “That strangers are friends that we some day may meet,” per Quote Investigator ↗.

Guest returned to the theme in his 1919 poem “The Unknown Friends,” writing that each of us has friends “he / Has yet to meet and really know… / Although they pass as strangers here,” according to the same investigation ↗.
By 1941, condensed and anonymous versions were running as unattributed newspaper filler in papers like Utah’s Park Record and Iowa’s Postville Herald, per Quote Investigator ↗.

The Yeats attribution itself first surfaces in a 1997 Usenet post with no citation, and popular crowdsourced sites like Goodreads ↗ compound the error by tagging it to Yeats’s 1922 memoir Four Years — a work that does not contain it.
source.excerptNote: This exact wording appears nowhere in Yeats's published work; it is the modern folk form documented by Quote Investigator.
source.rightsNote: Because the exact modern wording evolved anonymously through mid-20th-century newspaper filler rather than from one identifiable authored publication, its copyright status cannot be responsibly determined; it is not a Yeats work and no rights holder can be named.

author.name: Edgar A. Guest
author.kicker: Closest identifiable antecedent — not William Butler Yeats
author.heading: About Edgar A. Guest
author.metaLine: 1881–1959 · British-born American newspaper poet, "the People's Poet"
author.bio: Guest was a hugely popular syndicated newspaper poet who published an estimated 11,000 sentimental, optimistic poems in some 300 papers over four decades. His 1915 poem Faith and 1919 poem The Unknown Friends are the earliest identified sources for the “strangers are friends not yet met” sentiment, though not in the exact wording now attributed to Yeats.

misattribution.heading: Misattribution
misattribution.intro: This is one of the internet’s most durable false literary attributions — credited to Yeats on quote sites, in wedding toasts, and on tourism posters, despite no supporting citation ever surfacing.

items.scope: widespread on quote-aggregator sites, greeting cards, and hospitality marketing
items.why: Quote Investigator's dedicated research concludes flatly that “the attribution to William Butler Yeats is unsupported ↗”; the earliest traced instance is an uncited 1997 Usenet post, decades after the saying was already in circulation.

In 1996, Mark Victor Hansen's book Out of the Blue attached a nearly identical line — “Strangers are just friends I haven’t met yet” — to humorist Will Rogers, an attribution Quote Investigator ↗ also found unsupported.
Some sites, including Goodreads ↗, list the line as coming from Yeats's 1922 autobiographical volume Four Years, giving the false attribution a specific-sounding but unverifiable source.

misattribution.truthLine: The best-documented trail, per Quote Investigator ↗, runs from Edgar Guest's 1915 and 1919 poems, through anonymous 1941 newspaper filler, to an uncited 1997 attribution to Yeats — not a genuine Yeats quotation at all.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: This warm, welcoming line is one of the most widely shared “Yeats” quotes online — stitched onto travel-brand ads, wedding programs, and hospitality-industry posters. It certainly sounds like something the Irish poet might have said. But no biographer, editor, or archive has ever located it in his poems, plays, letters, or prose.

The real trail is far less tidy: a diffuse, decades-long folk evolution of a sentiment popularized by American newspaper poet Edgar Guest, gradually condensed into anonymous aphorism form by the early 1940s, and only linked to Yeats’s name more than half a century later — with no citation offered then or since.
context.pull: The Yeats attribution first appears, uncited, in a 1997 Usenet post — decades after the saying was already circulating anonymously in American newspapers.
